summary: Glenox Circular Materials, Inc., a lithium-ion battery recycler and the firm's client, licenses Protoux Analytics, Inc.'s 'Protoux CellTrace' battery chain-of-custody and materials-recovery analytics platform under a Software License Agreement governed by New York law. The license is for Glenox's Rochester, New York hydrometallurgical facility. The folder also holds a side letter granting a fee discount in exchange for exclusivity, a data processing addendum, a Glenox notice letter announcing the pending sale of Glenox to Sennford Resources Corp., a parent guaranty from Glenox Holdings LLC, an implementation statement of work, an order form, kickoff meeting notes and Protoux's certificate of insurance. Five issues are planted. (1) The cap carve-out in the license agreement leaves Glenox's indemnity in the data processing addendum uncapped. (2) The pending sale triggers a change of control consent right that Glenox has not sought. (3) Protoux may assign freely. (4) The side letter's exclusivity, read with the license agreement's definition of the operations it covers, reaches all Glenox affiliate operations worldwide. (5) The order form auto-renews for repeated five-year terms on a 120-day opt-out window.

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: The cap and the indemnity sit in different documents. Read alone, neither looks harmful; read together, they leave Glenox with unlimited liability. Section 9.2 of the Data Processing Addendum (D3) requires Glenox, as Customer, to 'indemnify, defend and hold harmless Processor' against all Losses, 'including regulatory fines'. The indemnity covers claims arising from Customer's processing instructions and from Customer's failure to give required notices or obtain required consents for personal data. That data includes drop-off customer, collection driver and employee data in battery chain-of-custody records. Section 10.1 of the DPA says liability under it is subject to the Agreement's limitations of liability, so on its own the DPA looks capped. But Section 11.3(b) of the License Agreement (D1) says the 12-month-fees cap in Section 11.1 'shall not apply to' 'either party's data protection obligations'. Section 1 of D1 defines that term to include all obligations under the Data Processing Addendum. Read alone, that carve-out looks mutual and favourable to Glenox, because it seems aimed at Protoux's data breaches. Together, the two provisions remove the cap from Glenox's broad DPA indemnity. Glenox is left with unlimited exposure, including for regulatory fines. Precedence does not cure this. The Agreement ranks above the DPA, but the two provisions do not conflict, so the Agreement's carve-out simply applies to the DPA indemnity.
issues.expected_finding: Section 11.3(b) of the License Agreement removes the Section 11.1 cap from all DPA obligations, so Glenox's indemnity of Protoux in DPA Section 9.2 (which covers regulatory fines) is uncapped despite DPA Section 10.1. The carve-out should be limited to Protoux's obligations, or Glenox's DPA indemnity made expressly subject to the cap (or a separate super-cap).
detect_terms2: indemnify, defend and hold harmless Processor

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: Section 1 of the License Agreement (D1) defines 'Change of Control of Licensee' to include any transfer of more than 50% of Licensee's voting shares. Section 15.2 makes any Change of Control of Licensee without Protoux's prior written consent a ground for Protoux to terminate on 10 days' notice. On termination, Protoux may also declare 'all unpaid Subscription Fees for the remainder of the Subscription Term' immediately due. Read alone, that is ordinary drafting. The notice letter (D4), dated October 20, 2026, is a courtesy letter from Glenox to Protoux. It reports that Glenox Holdings LLC signed a share purchase agreement on October 14, 2026 to sell all shares of Glenox to Sennford Resources Corp., with closing expected on or about January 15, 2027. The letter is expressly sent 'for information purposes only' and requests no consent. Read together, the sale is a Change of Control requiring Protoux's prior written consent, which has not been sought. That exposes Glenox to termination and acceleration of up to five years of fees at $480,000 a year under the Order Form (D7).
detect_terms: all unpaid Subscription Fees for the remainder of the Subscription Term
issues.expected_finding: The sale of Glenox to Sennford Resources Corp. disclosed in the October 20, 2026 notice letter is a Change of Control under License Agreement Section 15.2 that requires Protoux's prior written consent. Because the letter requests no consent, Glenox risks termination and acceleration of all remaining Subscription Fees. Glenox should obtain Protoux's written consent or waiver before the expected January 15, 2027 closing.

issues.label: unrestricted assignment
issues.description: Section 15.1 of the License Agreement (D1) bars Licensee from assigning without Licensor's prior written consent. It then provides that Licensor 'may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, without Licensee's consent' to any person, including by merger or sale of assets. Nothing limits assignees or requires notice. Protoux could therefore transfer the platform contract, together with Glenox's chain-of-custody and recovery-yield data held under it, to a competing battery recycler or a financially weaker vendor, and Glenox would have no consent right or termination right.
detect_terms: may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, without Licensee's consent
issues.expected_finding: Section 15.1 lets Protoux assign the License Agreement to anyone, including a competing battery recycler, without Glenox's consent while Glenox's own assignment requires consent. The clause should be made mutual, or at minimum Protoux's assignment should be limited to a successor of its whole business that is not a Glenox competitor, with notice to Glenox and a Glenox termination right.

issues.label: overbroad exclusivity
issues.description: Section 2 of the side letter (D2) grants Glenox a 15% fee discount. In exchange, Glenox agrees to use the Platform 'as its exclusive traceability and process analytics software for Covered Operations' and not to license, develop or use any competing software for Covered Operations during the Subscription Term. Read alone, the side letter looks tied to the licensed deployment. The side letter uses 'Covered Operations' as defined in the License Agreement. Section 1 of the License Agreement (D1) defines 'Covered Operations' as 'all battery collection, sorting, processing and materials recovery activities of Licensee and its Affiliates, wherever located'. Within D1 that definition only sets the scope of support and warranty coverage, so there its breadth helps Glenox. Read together, the exclusivity extends to every Glenox and affiliate operation worldwide. That would include lead-acid and other lines and, after the pending sale, potentially Sennford Resources Corp.'s operations as a new affiliate. The deal, however, licenses the Platform only for the Licensed Site, the Rochester, New York hydrometallurgical facility (Order Form D7, Section 2). Precedence does not help. The side letter does not conflict with the Agreement or the Order Form; it borrows the Agreement's definition.
detect_terms: exclusive traceability and process analytics software for Covered Operations
issues.expected_finding: Read with the License Agreement's definition of Covered Operations, the side letter's exclusivity bars Glenox and all its affiliates worldwide from using competing software, far beyond the single Rochester Licensed Site in the Order Form. The exclusivity should be limited to the Licensed Site and to the licensed lithium-ion processing activities, and should exclude any future acquirer's affiliates.
detect_terms2: Licensee and its Affiliates, wherever located

issues.label: automatic renewal
issues.description: Section 1 of the Order Form (D7) sets an Initial Subscription Term of 60 months. Section 4 provides that the subscription 'renews automatically for successive Renewal Terms equal in length to the Initial Subscription Term' unless a party gives notice of non-renewal at least 120 days before the end of the then-current term. Section 3.1 of the License Agreement (D1) defers to the Order Form on term, and the Order Form ranks first in the order of precedence. Reading Section 4 with Section 1 shows that each renewal locks Glenox in for another five years of fees at $480,000 a year, or $2.4 million per Renewal Term. Glenox can avoid this only through a 120-day window once every five years, and nothing in Section 4 requires Protoux to send a reminder.
detect_terms: renews automatically for successive Renewal Terms equal in length to the Initial Subscription Term
issues.expected_finding: Read with the 60-month Initial Subscription Term in Order Form Section 1, the Order Form auto-renews for successive five-year terms (about $2.4 million each) unless Glenox gives non-renewal notice at least 120 days before expiry. Glenox should negotiate renewals of no more than 12 months, a termination-for-convenience right after renewal, or a Protoux reminder obligation before the notice window.
